# Purpose and scope {#purpose}

This is a single living document maintained by members of the
[LENS Program](https://lens-program.github.io/lens-program/). It records how identifiability,
recoverability, and related ideas are defined in different fields, **each with its own
mathematical formulation**, so the frameworks can be compared directly. The aim is to find
where fields agree, where the same word means different things, and what is still unknown.

This is a **preliminary working resource**. Corrections, additions, and alternative
formulations are welcome, and nothing here is a LENS consensus unless the text says the group
agreed on it. Step-by-step instructions for editing this document and adding references are in
the [repository README](https://github.com/lens-program/collective-knowledge-base#how-to-contribute).

**Labels used throughout**

- *(proposed)*: a connection or interpretation offered by a contributor and not yet discussed.
- *(under discussion)*: raised at a LENS meeting or talk; the group has not settled it.
- *(resolved)*: the group discussed it and agreed; the text records what was agreed and when.

## Terminology at a glance {#at-a-glance}

| Concept | Core question | Perspectives currently represented |
|---|---|---|
| [Identifiability](#identifiability) | Is the target uniquely determined by the observable distribution? | Parametric statistics, econometrics, causal inference, dynamical systems, Bayesian inference |
| [Structural non-identifiability](#structural-non-identifiability) | Does the model itself prevent unique determination, even with perfect data? | Dynamical systems, statistical ecology, parametric statistics |
| [Practical identifiability](#practical-identifiability) | Can the target be estimated with useful precision from the data at hand? | Dynamical systems, econometrics, Bayesian inference |
| [Partial identification](#partial-identification) | When point identification fails, how far do the data narrow the target down? | Econometrics, Bayesian inference |
| [Recoverability](#recoverability) | Which targets can still be learned when the full model is not identifiable? | Missing data, causal inference, inverse problems; proposed LENS usage |

# Terminology and mathematical definitions {#concepts}

Each concept has a short core question, followed by one block per disciplinary perspective.
Every perspective gives its own definition, mathematical formulation, and references, so it can
be read on its own and compared with the others.

## Identifiability {#identifiability}

### Core question

If we knew the distribution of the observable data exactly, could we determine the target
quantity uniquely? Identifiability is a property of the **model and the observation scheme**,
not of a particular dataset or estimator.

### Perspective: Parametric statistical models

**Definition.** A model is identifiable when distinct parameter values imply distinct
distributions of the observable data.

**Mathematical formulation.** For a model $\mathcal{P} = \{P_\theta : \theta \in \Theta\}$:

$$
P_{\theta_1} = P_{\theta_2} \implies \theta_1 = \theta_2 \qquad \text{for all } \theta_1, \theta_2 \in \Theta .
$$

Common variants:

- **Local identifiability at $\theta_0$:** the implication holds for all $\theta_1, \theta_2$
  in some open neighbourhood of $\theta_0$.
- **Information-matrix criterion:** suppose the model is regular (smooth densities with common
  support, so that the information matrix $I(\theta)$ exists and is continuous), and $\theta_0$
  is a *regular point* of $I(\theta)$, meaning $I(\theta)$ has constant rank in a neighbourhood
  of $\theta_0$. Then $\theta_0$ is locally identifiable if and only if $I(\theta_0)$ is
  nonsingular. Without the regular-point condition, the equivalence can fail.
- **Generic identifiability:** identifiability holds for all $\theta$ outside a subset of
  $\Theta$ of Lebesgue measure zero.
- **Identifiability of a functional $\psi(\theta)$:** $P_{\theta_1} = P_{\theta_2} \implies
  \psi(\theta_1) = \psi(\theta_2)$. A functional can be identified when $\theta$ is not.

**References.** [@rothenberg1971identification; @paulino1994identifiability;
@allman2009identifiability]

*Contributed by:* Emily Peterson (2026-10-13)

### Perspective: Econometrics

**Definition.** The structural parameters of an economic model are identified if they can be
recovered uniquely from the distribution of observables. Classically, this means recovering them
from the reduced form.

**Mathematical formulation.** Suppose the distribution of observables depends on the structural
parameter $\theta$ only through a reduced-form parameter $\pi = g(\theta)$, and $\pi$ is
determined by that distribution. Then

$$
\theta \text{ is identified} \iff g \text{ is injective on } \Theta, \quad
\text{i.e. } g(\theta_1) = g(\theta_2) \implies \theta_1 = \theta_2 .
$$

The word "identification" covers many distinct notions in econometrics, including point, set,
local, generic, and weak identification. @lewbel2019identification surveys them.

**References.** [@koopmans1949identification; @lewbel2019identification]

*Contributed by:* Emily Peterson (2026-10-13)

### Perspective: Causal inference

**Definition.** A causal estimand is identifiable if it is uniquely determined by the
observed-data distribution under the assumed causal model.

**Mathematical formulation.** Let $\mathcal{M}$ be a class of causal models (e.g. all models
compatible with a given DAG), $\psi(M)$ the causal target, and $P_M$ the observed-data law
induced by $M$. Then

$$
P_{M_1} = P_{M_2} \implies \psi(M_1) = \psi(M_2) \qquad \text{for all } M_1, M_2 \in \mathcal{M} .
$$

The object being identified is an **estimand**, not necessarily a model parameter.

**References.** [@pearl2009causality]

*Contributed by:* Emily Peterson (2026-10-13)

### Perspective: Dynamical systems and systems biology

**Definition.** A model is *structurally* identifiable if its parameters are uniquely determined
by the model output under ideal conditions: noise-free, continuous observation of the measured
outputs.

**Mathematical formulation.** For a system

$$
\dot{x}(t) = f\big(x(t), \theta, u(t)\big), \qquad y(t) = h\big(x(t), \theta\big),
$$

with known initial conditions and inputs $u$ from an admissible class, the parameter $\theta$ is
globally structurally identifiable if

$$
y(t; \theta_1, u) = y(t; \theta_2, u) \ \text{ for all } t \ge 0 \text{ and all admissible } u
\implies \theta_1 = \theta_2 .
$$

It is locally structurally identifiable if this holds within a neighbourhood of each $\theta$.

**References.** [@bellman1970structural; @wieland2021structural]

*Contributed by:* Emily Peterson (2026-10-13)

### Perspective: Bayesian inference

**Definition.** Identifiability is not required for a proper posterior. With a proper prior, a
nonidentified model still has a well-defined posterior. Data can shift beliefs about
nonidentified parameters only *through* their prior dependence on identified ones.

**Mathematical formulation.** Write $\theta = (\theta_I, \theta_N)$, where the likelihood
depends on $\theta$ only through $\theta_I$: $p(y \mid \theta) = p(y \mid \theta_I)$. Then

$$
p(\theta_N \mid \theta_I, y) = p(\theta_N \mid \theta_I), \qquad
p(\theta_N \mid y) = \int p(\theta_N \mid \theta_I)\, p(\theta_I \mid y)\, d\theta_I .
$$

The data never update the *conditional* prior of $\theta_N$ given $\theta_I$. The *marginal*
posterior of $\theta_N$ can still differ from its prior if $\theta_N$ and $\theta_I$ are
dependent a priori.

**References.** [@poirier1998revising; @gustafson2015bayesian]

*Contributed by:* Emily Peterson (2026-10-13)

### Examples

- $Y \sim N(a + b, 1)$: $(a, b)$ is not identifiable, but $a + b$ is.
- Finite mixtures are identifiable at best up to relabelling of the components.
- Misclassified binary exposure: when sensitivity and specificity are unknown, prevalence is not
  identified from the error-prone measure alone. [@gustafson2005model]

### Connections and distinctions

- **Common structure across perspectives:** every formulation above has the form "equal
  observable law implies equal target". They differ in the target (parameter, reduced-form
  preimage, causal estimand, ODE parameter) and in the model class over which the implication
  must hold.
- **[Structural vs. practical](#structural-non-identifiability):** a model can be identifiable
  in principle and still [practically non-identifiable](#practical-identifiability) with
  finite, noisy data.
- **[Partial identification](#partial-identification):** when point identification fails, the
  data may still restrict the target to a set.
- **[Recoverability](#recoverability):** *(proposed)* recoverability asks which functionals
  can be learned, and may hold when the full parameter is not identifiable.
- **Observability** (control theory): whether the system *state* can be reconstructed from
  outputs. It is the state analogue of parameter identifiability. *(proposed; needs a reference
  and its own entry)*

### Open questions

- *(proposed)* Is there a common definition that covers parameters (statistics), estimands
  (causal inference), and states (control theory)? Or are these different questions?
- *(proposed)* How should "identified" be reported when identifiability holds generically but
  fails at the parameter values that matter scientifically, e.g. on a boundary?

## Structural non-identifiability {#structural-non-identifiability}

### Core question

Does the model structure itself prevent the target from being determined, even with perfect,
noise-free, unlimited data? Collecting more of the same data cannot fix structural
non-identifiability. Only changing the model, the observations, or the information supplied
(constraints, priors, external data) can.

### Perspective: Parametric statistical models

**Definition.** The model fails to be identifiable: distinct parameter values produce the same
distribution of the observables.

**Mathematical formulation.** There exist $\theta_1 \neq \theta_2$ in $\Theta$ with
$P_{\theta_1} = P_{\theta_2}$. Equivalently, for some $\theta_0$ the observational equivalence
class

$$
E(\theta_0) = \{\theta \in \Theta : P_\theta = P_{\theta_0}\}
$$

contains more than one point. $E(\theta_0)$ can take different forms:

- a **positive-dimensional set**, e.g. a curve or manifold, when parameters enter only through
  continuous combinations (as in $a + b$);
- a **finite or discrete set**, from discrete symmetries such as label switching in mixtures or
  sign changes of loadings in factor models.

$E(\theta_0)$ need not be bounded.

**References.** [@rothenberg1971identification]

*Contributed by:* Emily Peterson (2026-10-13)

### Perspective: Dynamical systems and systems biology

**Definition.** A parameter is structurally non-identifiable when ideal, noise-free model output
cannot determine it uniquely, typically because of a functional relationship among parameters.

**Mathematical formulation.** There exist $\theta_1 \neq \theta_2$ with $y(t; \theta_1, u) =
y(t; \theta_2, u)$ for all $t$ and all admissible inputs $u$.

As a diagnostic, @raue2009structural use the profile likelihood

$$
\mathrm{PL}(\theta_i) = \max_{\theta_{j \neq i}} L(\theta) .
$$

If the likelihood depends on $\theta$ only through identifiable combinations, it is constant
along the non-identifiable direction, so $\mathrm{PL}(\theta_i)$ is exactly flat in
$\theta_i$. This is the idealised structural case. In practice, numerically computed profiles may
look only approximately flat, depending on the optimiser and the profiling procedure. Discrete
non-identifiability (e.g. label switching) shows up instead as several equal maxima, not as a
flat profile.

**References.** [@bellman1970structural; @raue2009structural]

*Contributed by:* Emily Peterson (2026-10-13)

### Perspective: Statistical ecology (parameter redundancy)

**Definition.** A model is parameter-redundant if it can be rewritten in terms of fewer
parameters. A parameter-redundant model is not identifiable.

**Mathematical formulation.** Let $\kappa(\theta)$ be an *exhaustive summary*, i.e. a vector of
quantities that determines the model's distribution, with $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^p$. Form the
derivative matrix

$$
D(\theta) = \frac{\partial \kappa(\theta)}{\partial \theta}, \qquad r = \operatorname{rank} D(\theta) .
$$

The model is parameter-redundant if $r < p$. The **deficiency** $d = p - r$ is the number of
parameters that cannot be estimated, and $r$ is the number of estimable parameter
combinations.

**References.** [@catchpole1997detecting; @cole2020parameter]

*Contributed by:* Emily Peterson (2026-10-13)

### Examples

- $Y \sim N(a + b, 1)$: only $a + b$ is estimable; $p = 2$, $r = 1$, deficiency 1.
- Grouped or normalised likelihoods: if a likelihood depends on predictors only through
  within-group shares (e.g. a multinomial allocation within each group), any term that is
  constant within a group cancels and is structurally non-identifiable. An external anchor that
  varies within groups is needed to identify it.
- Capture–recapture models where survival and capture probability on the final occasion appear
  only as a product. [@catchpole1997detecting]
- Finite mixtures: relabelling the components gives a discrete equivalence class of size $K!$.

### Connections and distinctions

- **vs. [practical identifiability](#practical-identifiability):** structural problems come from
  the model and persist with infinite data. Practical problems come from limited, noisy data.
- **[Partial identification](#partial-identification):** the equivalence class $E(\theta_0)$ is
  the identified set. It may be bounded or unbounded, and continuous or discrete. Partial
  identification studies its size and shape, often under extra assumptions that shrink it.
- **[Recoverability](#recoverability):** *(proposed)* the estimable combinations are the
  functionals that remain point-recoverable.

### Open questions

- *(proposed)* Symbolic rank methods scale poorly. What is the right check for high-dimensional
  hierarchical or spatial models with thousands of latent effects?

## Practical identifiability {#practical-identifiability}

### Core question

The model may be identifiable in principle. But with the finite, noisy data we actually have,
can the target be estimated precisely enough to be useful? Practical non-identifiability is a
property of the **model together with the data**, and more or better data can fix it.

There is no single, framework-free definition. Each perspective below gives a **field-specific
operational criterion**.

### Perspective: Dynamical systems and systems biology

**Definition.** A structurally identifiable parameter is practically non-identifiable if its
likelihood-based confidence interval, given the available data, extends to infinity in at
least one direction.

**Mathematical formulation.** With profile likelihood $\mathrm{PL}(\theta_i)$ and maximum
likelihood estimate $\hat\theta$, the profile-likelihood confidence region at level $1-\alpha$
is

$$
\mathrm{CI}_{1-\alpha}(\theta_i) = \Big\{ \theta_i : -2 \log \frac{\mathrm{PL}(\theta_i)}{L(\hat\theta)} < \chi^2_{1,\,1-\alpha} \Big\} .
$$

$\theta_i$ is practically non-identifiable if this region is unbounded above or below.

**References.** [@raue2009structural; @wieland2021structural]

*Contributed by:* Emily Peterson (2026-10-13)

### Perspective: Econometrics (weak identification)

**Definition.** A parameter is weakly identified when the data carry little information about
it. In instrumental-variable and GMM settings, this happens when the instruments are only weakly
related to the endogenous variables, and standard asymptotic approximations become unreliable.

**Mathematical formulation.** In the linear IV model

$$
y = X\beta + u, \qquad X = Z\pi + v,
$$

weak instruments are modelled as local to zero, $\pi = C / \sqrt{n}$ for fixed $C$, so the
strength of identification does not grow with the sample size. Under this sequence, the
two-stage least squares estimator is not consistent and its usual normal approximation fails.

**References.** [@staiger1997instrumental; @stock2002survey]

*Contributed by:* Emily Peterson (2026-10-13)

### Perspective: Bayesian inference

**Definition.** One working criterion is that a parameter is weakly identified by the data when
its posterior remains dominated by the prior. This is one operational check, not a definition.

**Mathematical formulation.** The prior–posterior overlap for a parameter $\theta_j$ is

$$
\tau_j = \int \min\big\{ p(\theta_j),\ p(\theta_j \mid y) \big\}\, d\theta_j \in [0, 1] ,
$$

and large values flag parameters about which the data say little. @garrett2000latent use this
diagnostic in latent class models.

**References.** [@garrett2000latent]

*Contributed by:* Emily Peterson (2026-10-13)

### Examples

- An ODE model where a rate constant can be estimated only if the system is sampled during a
  fast transient that the design misses.
- Hierarchical models with few groups: the between-group variance is identifiable but very
  poorly estimated.
- Instrumental-variable analysis with a weak first stage. [@stock2002survey]

### Connections and distinctions

- **vs. [structural non-identifiability](#structural-non-identifiability):** in the structural
  case the profile likelihood is flat for every dataset. In the practical case it is finite but
  wide or one-sided for the data at hand.
- **Across perspectives:** the three criteria answer different questions. The profile
  likelihood measures interval width, weak-instrument asymptotics measure how identification
  strength scales with $n$, and prior–posterior overlap measures prior dominance. They need not
  agree. *(proposed)*
- **[Recoverability](#recoverability):** *(proposed)* practical identifiability is to
  identifiability what precise recovery is to recoverability.

### Open questions

- *(proposed)* Is there a definition of practical identifiability that is not tied to a
  particular inferential framework (likelihood, GMM, Bayesian)?
- *(proposed)* How should practical identifiability be assessed for spatial and hierarchical
  models, where information varies across components and locations?

## Partial identification {#partial-identification}

### Core question

Point identification fails. Can the observable distribution, together with credible
assumptions, still restrict the target to a set, and how small is that set?

### Perspective: Econometrics

**Definition.** A parameter is partially identified when the observable distribution, combined
with the maintained assumptions, restricts it to a set (the *identified set*) that is larger than
a point but smaller than the whole parameter space. The emphasis is on weak, credible
assumptions that yield bounds, rather than strong assumptions that yield a point.

**Mathematical formulation.** With observed-data distribution $P_0$:

$$
\Theta_I = \{\theta \in \Theta : P_\theta = P_0\}, \qquad
\Psi_I = \{\psi(\theta) : \theta \in \Theta_I\} .
$$

In many applications $\Theta_I$ is defined by moment inequalities, $\Theta_I = \{\theta :
E_{P_0}[m(W, \theta)] \le 0\}$. Point identification is the special case where $\Psi_I$ is a
single point.

**References.** [@manski2003partial; @tamer2010partial]

*Contributed by:* Emily Peterson (2026-10-13)

### Perspective: Bayesian inference

**Definition.** In a partially identified model, the posterior does not concentrate on a point
as $n \to \infty$. It converges to a limiting distribution over the identified set, whose shape
is determined by the prior.

**Mathematical formulation.** Use a *transparent* reparameterisation $\theta \mapsto (\phi,
\lambda)$, where the likelihood depends only on $\phi$. Then

$$
p(\phi, \lambda \mid y) = p(\phi \mid y)\, p(\lambda \mid \phi),
$$

and as $n \to \infty$, $p(\phi \mid y)$ concentrates at the true $\phi_0$. The limiting posterior
of $\lambda$ is therefore the conditional prior $p(\lambda \mid \phi_0)$, supported on the
identified set.

@moon2012bayesian show that, asymptotically, Bayesian credible sets for a partially identified
parameter can be strictly smaller than frequentist confidence sets for its identified set.

**References.** [@gustafson2015bayesian; @moon2012bayesian]

*Contributed by:* Emily Peterson (2026-10-13)

### Examples

- Mean of an outcome $Y \in [0, 1]$ with missing values (missingness indicator $D = 1$ when
  observed) and no assumption about the missingness mechanism:

  $$
  E[Y \mid D=1]\,P(D=1) \;\le\; E[Y] \;\le\; E[Y \mid D=1]\,P(D=1) + P(D=0) .
  $$

  [@manski2003partial]
- Misclassification with sensitivity and specificity known only to lie in ranges.
  [@gustafson2005model]

### Connections and distinctions

- **[Identifiability](#identifiability):** point identification is the degenerate case.
- **[Structural non-identifiability](#structural-non-identifiability):** the observational
  equivalence class is the identified set when no further assumptions are added. It need not be
  bounded or of positive dimension.
- **[Recoverability](#recoverability):** *(proposed)* a functional constant over $\Theta_I$ is
  point-recoverable. A functional whose identified set $\Psi_I$ is a proper subset of its range
  is recoverable only up to bounds, which is a weaker property.

### Open questions

- *(proposed)* How should we report uncertainty when part of it can be reduced with more data
  and part of it never can?

## Recoverability {#recoverability}

### Core question

Given the data and the model we have, which targets can be learned (recovered), even when the
model as a whole is not identifiable?

"Recoverability" is used in several established, field-specific senses, listed first below. A
broader LENS usage is listed separately and is explicitly *proposed*.

### Perspective: Missing data (graphical models)

**Definition.** A target quantity (e.g. a joint distribution or a causal effect) is recoverable
if it can be computed consistently from the distribution of the observed, partially missing
data, given the assumptions encoded in a missingness graph (m-graph).

**Mathematical formulation.** Let $G$ be an m-graph and $P^{\text{obs}}_M$ the distribution of
the observed portion of the data, including the missingness indicators, under model $M$. A
query $Q$ is recoverable if

$$
P^{\text{obs}}_{M_1} = P^{\text{obs}}_{M_2} \implies Q(M_1) = Q(M_2)
\qquad \text{for all } M_1, M_2 \text{ compatible with } G .
$$

**References.** [@mohan2013graphical]

*Contributed by:* Emily Peterson (2026-10-13)

### Perspective: Causal inference (selection bias and data fusion)

**Definition.** A query is recoverable from selection-biased data if it can be computed from the
distribution of the selected sample, possibly together with external unbiased data, under the
assumptions in the causal graph.

**Mathematical formulation.** Let $S$ indicate selection into the sample, and let $G$ be a
causal graph that includes $S$. The query $Q$ (e.g. $P(y \mid x)$) is recoverable from selection
bias if

$$
P_{M_1}(v \mid S = 1) = P_{M_2}(v \mid S = 1) \implies Q(M_1) = Q(M_2)
\qquad \text{for all } M_1, M_2 \text{ compatible with } G ,
$$

with the hypothesis extended to include any external distributions that are available.

**References.** [@bareinboim2014recovering; @bareinboim2016causal]

*Contributed by:* Emily Peterson (2026-10-13)

### Perspective: Inverse problems and compressed sensing

**Definition.** "Recovery" means reconstructing a signal exactly or stably from incomplete
measurements, under structural conditions such as sparsity.

**Mathematical formulation.** Observe $y = A x$, where $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ with $m
< n$, and $x$ has at most $s$ nonzero entries. $x$ is exactly recovered by

$$
\hat{x} = \arg\min_{z} \|z\|_1 \quad \text{subject to } A z = y
$$

if $\hat{x} = x$. For randomly sampled Fourier measurements, exact recovery holds with high
probability once $m$ exceeds a constant multiple of $s \log n$.

**References.** [@candes2006robust]

*Contributed by:* Emily Peterson (2026-10-13)

### Proposed LENS usage

*(proposed; not an established definition)* LENS uses "recoverability" broadly, to ask which
**functionals** of a non-identifiable or partially identified model can be learned. Several
distinct properties are in play, and they should be kept separate:

| Property | Formulation | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **Point recoverability** | $\psi$ is identified: $P_{\theta_1} = P_{\theta_2} \implies \psi(\theta_1) = \psi(\theta_2)$ | Equivalent to identifiability of a functional |
| **Recoverability up to bounds** | the identified set $\Psi_I$ is a proper subset of the range of $\psi$ | Weaker than point recoverability; see [partial identification](#partial-identification) |
| **Posterior learning** | $p(\psi \mid y) \neq p(\psi)$ | *Not* a criterion for recoverability. The posterior can change through prior dependence on identified parameters, even when $\psi$ is not identified by the likelihood |
| **Posterior concentration** | $p(\psi \mid y)$ concentrates at a point as $n \to \infty$ | Related to point recoverability, but the relationship needs discussion *(under discussion)* |

### Examples

- $Y \sim N(a + b, 1)$: $a + b$ is point-recoverable; $a$ is not recoverable at all without
  bounds on $a$ or $b$.
- Recovering a population distribution from a selected sample when selection depends only on
  measured variables. [@bareinboim2014recovering]
- Exact recovery of a sparse signal from far fewer Fourier coefficients than the signal length.
  [@candes2006robust]

### Connections and distinctions

- **vs. [identifiability](#identifiability):** in causal inference and missing-data work,
  "recoverable" is close to "identifiable" in a specific data setting (missingness, selection).
  *(proposed)*
- **Point recovery vs. bounds:** a functional constant over the identified set is
  point-recoverable. Others may be recoverable only up to bounds. These are different
  properties and should be reported differently.
- **Posterior learning vs. recovery:** a posterior that differs from its prior shows only that
  the data are informative through the prior structure, not that the target is recovered.
- **[Practical identifiability](#practical-identifiability):** a point-recoverable functional
  can still be estimated imprecisely.

### Open questions

- *(proposed)* Should LENS adopt one definition of recoverability, or keep several labelled
  ones (graphical, set-valued, Bayesian)?
- *(proposed)* How can recoverability be diagnosed in practice for complex hierarchical, spatial,
  or measurement-error models?
- *(proposed)* When, if ever, does posterior concentration of $\psi$ imply point
  recoverability, and vice versa?

# Connections across fields {#connections}

This section maps how the concepts relate, and where different fields use different words for
similar ideas. Rows marked *(proposed)* are interpretations awaiting discussion, not settled
correspondences.

## How the concepts relate

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  ID["Identifiability<br/>(point)"]
  SNI["Structural<br/>non-identifiability"]
  PI["Partial<br/>identification"]
  PRI["Practical<br/>identifiability"]
  REC["Recoverability<br/>(of functionals)"]
  SNI -- "failure of" --> ID
  SNI -- "equivalence class = identified set" --> PI
  ID -- "with finite, noisy data" --> PRI
  PI -- "functionals constant on the set" --> REC
  ID -- "of a functional" --> REC
```

## Rough equivalences between fields

| Idea | Statistics | Econometrics | Causal inference / missing data | Systems biology | Ecology |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Model determines the target uniquely | identifiability | (point) identification | identification; recoverability | structural identifiability | — |
| Model cannot determine it, even with infinite data | non-identifiability | under-identification | non-identifiable estimand | structural non-identifiability | parameter redundancy |
| Data carry little information about it | weak information *(proposed)* | weak identification | — | practical non-identifiability | near-redundancy |
| Target restricted to a set | — | partial / set identification | bounds | — | — |
| Some functions still learnable | identified functionals / estimable functions | — | recoverable queries | identifiable combinations | estimable combinations |

Empty cells are invitations: if your field has a term, add it.

## Same word, different meaning

- **"Identification"** in causal inference concerns an *estimand* given a causal model. In
  parametric statistics it concerns *parameters* given a probability model.
  [@pearl2009causality; @rothenberg1971identification]
- **"Recovery"** in compressed sensing means reconstructing a signal under sparsity. In
  missing-data work it means computing a quantity from the observed-data distribution.
  [@candes2006robust; @mohan2013graphical]
- **"Structural"** means "intrinsic to the model equations" in systems biology, but "the causal
  or economic model behind the reduced form" in econometrics.
  [@bellman1970structural; @koopmans1949identification]

# Open questions {#open-questions-all}

Questions LENS cannot yet answer, collected from talks, the concepts above, and discussion. Each
item carries a status label ([see Purpose and scope](#purpose)) and says where it was raised.
When a question is resolved, or turns into a project, update its label and note the outcome
here rather than deleting it.

## From the LENS charter

These are the questions on the [LENS Program page](https://lens-program.github.io/lens-program/).
All are *(proposed)*.

1. What are the relationships among identifiability, partial identifiability, practical
   identifiability, and recoverability?
2. Which parameters or functionals remain recoverable when a full model is nonidentifiable?
3. How can recoverability be characterized or diagnosed?
4. How do priors, constraints, measurement error, and external information affect what can be
   learned?
5. How do spatial and hierarchical structures influence identifiability?
6. How do likelihood-based and objective-function approaches relate?
7. How should we represent uncertainty when information varies across model components?
